title: Linen and Eye Paint
objective: After this level you can explain Egyptian clothes and why both men and women wore makeup.
summary: Egyptians dressed in linen woven from flax. Men and women both wore green and black eye paint, for beauty, the gods and health; a 2010 lab study hints it may have helped fight infection.

cards.headline: In ancient Egypt, men wore eyeliner too. And they had reasons.
cards.body: Cosmetics were worn by both sexes, and the eyes got the most attention. The clothes were simple. The makeup may have done more than look good.

cards.headline: Dressed in flax
cards.body: Level 4’s flax crop ended up on people’s backs. Linen, woven from flax, was Egypt’s chief textile; wool was used more rarely, for things like warm cloaks. Men wore a short skirt tied at the waist. Women wore a sheath-like gown that ran from the ankles to just below the breasts. Light cloth for a hot country: the dress code was basically “linen, and not much of it.”

cards.headline: Green and black
cards.body: Egyptians wore green eye shadow made from powdered malachite and black or gray eyeliner. One ingredient of dark eye paint was galena, a lead sulfide mineral. Why bother? Egyptians thought eye paint looked good and pleased the gods, and they also believed it was healthy: it was said to keep off disease-carrying flies and block the sun’s glare. Beauty, religion and sunglasses in one.

cards.headline: What the lab found
cards.body: In 2010, French chemists tested lead compounds from Egyptian makeup on human skin cells in the lab. The compounds raised the cells’ output of nitric oxide, which helps the immune system fight bacteria, by up to 240 percent. That hints the makeup could have helped against eye infections. It isn’t proof it worked on real eyes, and lead is toxic: today the US FDA warns that lead-containing kohl can cause lead poisoning.
cards.callout: A clue from a lab dish, not a prescription.
